optionReasons.saa-ini-064:option:1: st1 is HDD for sequential throughput (big data/logs) — no SSD for general use.
optionReasons.saa-ini-064:option:2: i2 is for IOPS provisioned from critical banks — maximum performance with higher cost, excessive for moderate load.
optionReasons.saa-ini-064:option:3: sc1 is the HDD FRIO cheaper and slower — unsuitable for web server.

finalJustifications: Because gp3 is the SSD current general use: 3.000 IOPS and 125 Base MB/s in any size, with IOPS/separately available throughput — better common cost-benefit.
Because gp3 automatically doubles performance when the volume fills, compensating for the cost of IOPS Additional provisions.
Because gp3 is the only volume compatible with the burstable instances T3, the standard pair for moderate load web servers.
Because gp3 uses the RAM of the instance as a reading cache, delivering the performance of SSD with the price of a HDD common magnetic.

optionReasons.saa-ini-065:option:0: st1 is HDD — does not deliver tens of thousands of IOPS.
optionReasons.saa-ini-065:option:1: Forum Store is ephemeral — data goes down with instance; unacceptable for critical bank.
optionReasons.saa-ini-065:option:3: gp3 reaches 16.000 IOPS — below required; and the durability of the yo2 (99,999%) is superior.

finalJustifications: Because the Io2/io2 Block Express delivers IOPS (up to hundreds of thousands) with durability of 99,999% — designed for critical banks.
Because the yo2 replicates the volume to three different regions, and it is this geographical redundancy that guarantees the durability.
'Cause yo2 is the only volume EBS with factory-enabled encryption, the critical database requirement.
Because io2 uses physical host memory as main storage, recording to disk only asynchronously.

optionReasons.saa-ini-066:option:1: The sc1 is the HDD FRIO: cheaper, but much lower throughput — for rarely accessed data, not intense lot reading.
optionReasons.saa-ini-066:option:2: The gp3 attends, but costs more per GB — for pure sequential throughput the HDD optimized gains in cost-benefit.
optionReasons.saa-ini-066:option:3: i2 is for IOPS random critical banks — pay IOPS provided for sequential reading is waste.

finalJustifications: Because st1 is the HDD optimized for THROUGHPUT sequential (big data, logs) with cost per GB much lower than SSDs — the exact fit of the pattern described.
Because st1 is a SSD high-speed with IOPS provided, dimensioned for sequential readings of large batches.
Because the st1 automatically replicates the logs to the S3, combining the low cost of the bucket with the performance of the local block.
Because st1 is the only volume EBS which grows in size alone, following the continuous accumulation of log files.

optionReasons.saa-ini-067:option:0: It seems close because the CRR is also a resource of the S3 which involves moving data between remote locations — but it replicates objects DEPOIS that the upload has already reached the bucket; who speeds up the sending of those who are far away, routing through the Edge Locations, is the Transfer Acceleration.
optionReasons.saa-ini-067:option:1: Lifecycle moves objects between classes by age — nothing to do with shipping speed.
optionReasons.saa-ini-067:option:3: Intelligent-Tiering Optimizes CUSTO storage — not the upload network path.

finalJustifications: Because the Transfer Acceleration makes the upload go through Edge Location closer to the sender and follow the backbone of the AWS even the pocket — real gain in long distances.
Because Transfer Acceleration compresses files during shipment, reducing gigabytes that cross the internet to Oregon.
Because Transfer Acceleration creates a mirror pocket on each continent, and local uploads are consolidated in the main early-morning pocket.
Because Transfer Acceleration prioritizes customer traffic on the public internet, buying dedicated band from local operators.

optionReasons.saa-ini-068:option:1: Batch Operations executes mass actions on objects EXISTENTES (copy, restore, tags) — is not upload technique.
optionReasons.saa-ini-068:option:2: One ZIP only becomes a monolithic upload — a failure in the end restarts everything, the opposite of the desired.
optionReasons.saa-ini-068:option:3: Anonymous tab changes absolutely nothing in the upload mechanism.

finalJustifications: Because the multipart upload divides the object into parts sent in parallel and retransmits only the part that failed — recommended practice from ~100 MB.
Because the multipart upload sends the file across multiple regions at the same time, adding the band from each route to the bucket.
Because the multipart upload eliminates the limit of 5 TB by object, dividing larger files into objects chained in the pocket.
Because the multipart upload encrypts each part with a different key, protecting the file during parallel sending.

optionReasons.saa-ini-086:option:0: A CRR replica to another Region (DR) — does not move objects to cheaper classes.
optionReasons.saa-ini-086:option:1: Transfer Acceleration Accelerate uploads — Does Not Manage Object Aging.
optionReasons.saa-ini-086:option:3: Version preserves versions — does not pass objects between classes according to age.

finalJustifications: Because the lifecycle policy programs transitions by age (Standard-IA to 90 days, Glacier after) and expiration at the end of 5 years — automatic optimization.
Because lifecycle policy compacts old reports into files ZIP, reducing cost without changing storage class.
Because lifecycle policy automatically excludes unconsulted reports from 30 days, keeping only the taxes active.
Because the lifecycle policy notify the team to approve each transition, ensuring manual control of legal retention.

optionReasons.saa-ini-087:option:0: One Zone-IA reduces redundancy to UMA AZ and recovery snake — wrong for unpredictable and valuable access data.
optionReasons.saa-ini-087:option:1: Deep Archive has hours of waiting and recovery rate — unfeasible for objects that can be accessed again.
optionReasons.saa-ini-087:option:3: Standard forever is paying dearly for millions of cold objects — without any optimization.

finalJustifications: Because Intelligent-Tiering monitors each object and automatically moves it between layers according to actual use, without recovery rates — made for unpredictable patterns.
Because the Intelligent-Tiering deletes the passing objects 90 days without access, cutting the cost of the date lake by the root of the problem.
Because Intelligent-Tiering uses ML to predict which objects will be deleted, archiving them before the final deletion of the bucket.
Because Intelligent-Tiering is free for more than 1 million objects, the incentive of AWS for large lake data.

optionReasons.saa-ini-088:option:0: Standard-IA is for access INFREQUENTE but still immediate — it costs far more than deep filing.
optionReasons.saa-ini-088:option:2: Instant Retrieval offers access in milliseconds — you pay for agility that the scenario dispenses (12h acceptable).
optionReasons.saa-ini-088:option:3: Standard is the most expensive class for data that will almost never be read.

finalJustifications: Because Deep Archive is the cheapest class in AWS, for the retention of 7-10+ years almost without access, with recovery in up 12 hours — the exact scenario.
Because Deep Archive returns data in milliseconds when requested, keeping the minimum cost of deep archiving.
Because the Deep Archive becomes free after the fifth year of retention, the progressive discount of long-term archiving.
Because Deep Archive migrates records to managed physical media, the cheapest means of retention of the required decade.
